title: System Design

lessons.title: How a Request Travels
lessons.summary: Follow a page load from the browser to the server and back.

steps.title: Start with a page load
steps.html:
You open a book page in an online store. The browser needs to:

  1. Find the server.
  2. Open a connection.
  3. Request the page.

Assumption. The browser has no cached DNS answer or open connection.

Example state

Item State
DNS No cache entry
Connection Closed
Request Waiting

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. Empty DNS cache.
diagram.caption: The first visit starts with an empty browser cache and no open connection.

steps.title: Find the address
steps.html:
The browser needs an IP address for the store's domain.

  1. Check the browser's cache.
  2. If there is no valid answer, ask a DNS resolver.
  3. The resolver checks its cache or queries other DNS servers.

Key idea. The time to live (TTL) tells a cache how long it can reuse a DNS answer.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address found
Connection Closed
Request Waiting

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. DNS resolver (added) (in focus): Finds the server address. Cache the reply until expiry. Flow: Browser to DNS resolver: Resolve domain. DNS resolver to Browser: Return IP address.
diagram.caption: The DNS reply gives the browser an address. The resolver can answer from its own cache.

steps.title: Open a secure connection
steps.html:
The browser opens a TCP connection. It then starts a TLS handshake.

During the handshake, the browser checks the server certificate. Both sides establish encryption keys.

Note. Setup takes time before the first HTTP request. The browser can often reuse the connection.

Key idea. A round trip includes the time for a message to reach the server and for a reply to return.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection TLS ready
Request Waiting

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. Verify the server certificate. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (added) (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Flow: Browser to Web server: Start TCP and TLS. Web server to Browser: Finish handshake.
diagram.caption: This example uses TCP and TLS. Connection setup comes before the HTTP request.

steps.title: Send the HTTP request
steps.html:
The browser sends GET /books/42.

The server reads the path. It sends the request to the product page handler.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection TLS ready
Request GET sent

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Route to the book handler. Flow: Browser to Web server: GET /books/42.
diagram.caption: The request path tells the server which book page to build.

steps.title: Read the product data
steps.html:
The application asks the database for the book's title, price, and stock status.

The database returns the matching record. The application uses it to build the page.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection TLS ready
Request Reading data

diagram.alt: Browser (context): Opens the book page. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Database (added) (in focus): Stores book records. One query on the critical path. Flow: Web server to Database: Query book 42. Database to Web server: Title and stock.
diagram.caption: The database sends the product record to the application.

steps.title: Receive the response
steps.html:
The server sends:

  • The HTTP status
  • The response headers
  • The HTML

The browser can start parsing the HTML before it receives the entire response.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection TLS ready
Request HTML arriving

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. Parse the HTML. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Database (context): Stores book records. Flow: Web server to Browser: Return 200 and HTML.
diagram.caption: The response path runs from the application back to the browser.

steps.title: Load the other files
steps.html:
The HTML points to more files. Examples include stylesheets, scripts, and the cover image.

  • Use valid cached copies.
  • Request the remaining files.

Note. Some sites serve these files from a separate host.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection Reused
Request Fetching files

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. Reuse the connection. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Database (context): Stores book records. Flow: Browser to Web server: Request assets. Web server to Browser: Return assets.
diagram.caption: The browser can request several page resources over the existing connection.

steps.title: Diagnose a slow database query
steps.html:
The browser connects quickly. Most of the request time is in the book lookup.

Use To find
Server trace The database call and its duration
Query plan How the database searched for the row

Key idea. An index on a frequently queried field can reduce lookup time. Check the query plan and measure the result.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection Reused
Request Slow database read

diagram.alt: Browser (context): Opens the book page. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Database (in focus): Stores book records. Inspect the query plan. Flow: Web server to Database: Query book 42. Database to Web server: Slow query result.
diagram.caption: Inspect the database part of the trace before adding application servers.

steps.title: Compare users in different regions
steps.html:
A distant visitor can wait longer even when the server does the same work. Each network round trip adds delay.

Compare timings from two regions. A CDN can serve eligible files closer to a visitor.

Example state

Item State
DNS Address known
Connection TLS ready
Request Longer network path

diagram.alt: Browser (in focus): Opens the book page. Longer round-trip time. DNS resolver (context): Finds the server address. Web server (in focus): Handles HTTP requests. Database (context): Stores book records. Flow: Browser to Web server: Send request. Web server to Browser: Delayed response.
diagram.caption: A distant visitor pays the extra delay on each network round trip.

steps.title: Review the timing
steps.html:
Compare browser timings for:

  • DNS lookup and connection setup
  • Time to the first response byte
  • Download time

Use a server trace to see how much time the application and database spent.

Key idea. Repeat the measurement with a warm cache and an existing connection. The browser can skip some of the work from the first load.

Example state

Item State
DNS Cacheable
Connection Reusable
Request Page loaded

Database (in focus): Stores book records. Flow: Browser to DNS resolver: Resolve if needed. Browser to Web server: Connect and request. Web server to Database: Look up book. Database to Web server: Return record. Web server to Browser: Return the page.
diagram.caption: Compare a first visit with a repeat visit to see which work the browser can skip.

lessons.title: Latency & Throughput
lessons.summary: Use latency, throughput, and concurrency to find and relieve bottlenecks.

steps.title: Measure a request
steps.html:
Latency is the elapsed time for one operation. Assume these steps run in order:

Work Time
Network travel 20 ms
Service processing 30 ms
Database call 70 ms
Total 120 ms

Note. When branches run in parallel, add the longest branch to the work they share.

Example state

Item State
Load One request
Latency 120 ms example
Throughput One completion

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Service (in focus): Processes requests. 30 ms processing. Database (in focus): Reads the source records. Flow: Clients to Service: Send one request. Service to Database: Read source record. Database to Service: Return after 70 ms. Service to Clients: Reply after 120 ms.
diagram.caption: Latency spans the time from request start until the client receives the response.

steps.title: Count completed work
steps.html:
Throughput is completed work per unit of time.

6,000 completions ÷ 60 seconds = 100 requests/s.

Requests can run at the same time even when each takes a long time. Count failures separately. When the queue grows, arrivals outpace completions.

Example state

Item State
Load 6,000 completions/min
Latency Varies per request
Throughput 100 requests/s

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Count over 60 seconds. Service (in focus): Processes requests. Database (context): Reads the source records. Flow: Clients to Service: Parallel requests. Service to Clients: 6,000 completions.
diagram.caption: Throughput counts completed operations in a time interval.

steps.title: Read the tail
steps.html:
A p95 of 120 ms means roughly 95% of requests finished within 120 ms. The result depends on the percentile method. The slowest requests can take much longer.

Record the workload and time window. Report p99 and errors as well as the mean.

Warning. Combine samples or histogram buckets across instances. Averaging each instance's percentile generally gives the wrong result.

Example state

Item State
Load 100 requests
Latency p95 = 120 ms
Throughput Measure the tail

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. p95 is about 120 ms. Service (in focus): Processes requests. Database (context): Reads the source records. Flow: Clients to Service: Send 100 requests. Service to Clients: Collect timings.
diagram.caption: The percentile describes a distribution, not the duration of every request.

steps.title: Relate latency and concurrency
steps.html:
In a stable system:

Average requests in flight = throughput × average latency.

At 100 completions/s and 0.12 s average latency, about 12 requests are in flight.

Note. Use the same system boundary and time units. This average does not predict the worst burst.

Example state

Item State
Load 100 requests/s
Latency 0.12 s average
Throughput 12 requests in flight

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Service (in focus): Processes requests. 12 requests in flight on average. Database (context): Reads the source records. Flow: Clients to Service: Send concurrently. Service to Clients: Complete 100/s.
diagram.caption: Requests overlap while the system processes them.

steps.title: Find the queue
steps.html:
The system receives 120 requests/s. The database finishes 100/s.

If all requests stay in the queue, the backlog grows by 20 requests/s. That is 1,200 more requests after one minute.

Measure queue depth and wait time. Longer timeouts do not increase database capacity.

Example state

Item State
Load Arrival exceeds capacity
Latency Tail latency rises
Throughput Backlog grows

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Service (in focus): Processes requests. Database (in focus): Reads the source records. Queue (added) (in focus): Holds waiting work. Backlog grows by 20/s. Flow: Clients to Service: Arrival: 120/s. Service to Queue: Queue work. Queue to Database: Drain: 100/s.
diagram.caption: Work waits in the queue when the database completes requests more slowly than they arrive.

steps.title: Change the bottleneck
steps.html:
Assume a cache serves 50% of 120 reads/s. Only 60 reads/s reach the database. Its assumed capacity is 100/s.

Measure p95, p99, cache hit rate, and database saturation after the change.

Warning. A cold cache or a burst of misses can overload the database. If writes are the bottleneck, a read cache may help little.

Example state

Item State
Load 120 requests/s
Latency Measure after change
Throughput 60 database reads/s

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Service (in focus): Processes requests. Database (in focus): Reads the source records. 60 reads/s on misses. Queue (context): Holds waiting work. Cache (added) (in focus): Serves repeated reads. Assume 50% hit rate. Flow: Clients to Service: Arrive: 120 reads/s. Service to Cache: Look up cache. Service to Database: Read on a miss.
diagram.caption: With the assumed hit rate, half of the requests avoid a database read.

steps.title: Recap: interpret the numbers
steps.html:
Measure Example and use
Latency 120 ms for one request. Find where it spends time.
Throughput 6,000/min = 100/s. Count completed requests.
Concurrency 100/s × 0.12 s = 12 in flight on average.
Backlog 120/s − 100/s = 20/s more queued.
Cache 120/s × 50% misses = 60/s store reads.

Check. State the workload and time window. Test under realistic load and check the tail, even if average latency improves.

Example state

Item State
Load Compare arrival and completion
Latency Track percentiles
Throughput Verify under load

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Send and time requests. Record p95 and p99. Service (in focus): Processes requests. Database (in focus): Reads the source records. Queue (in focus): Holds waiting work. Watch for backlog under load. Cache (in focus): Serves repeated reads. Flow: Clients to Service: Measure arrivals. Service to Cache: Measure hit rate. Service to Database: Measure store reads. Service to Clients: Count completions. Service to Queue: Observe backlog.
diagram.caption: Measure each component and the end-to-end path to locate waiting and saturation.

lessons.title: Napkin Math
lessons.summary: Turn explicit workload assumptions into traffic, bandwidth, and storage estimates.

steps.title: Define the example
steps.html:
Assume a photo service has 1 million daily active users. Each person:

  • Views 20 photos per day
  • Uploads one photo per day

Units. This example uses decimal sizes. 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. 1 TB = 1,000 GB.

Example state

Item State
Input 1M daily users
Estimate Estimate next
Decision State assumptions

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Assume 1M daily users. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. Flow: Users to Photo service: View or upload.
diagram.caption: Users produce requests; the service must handle both normal and peak traffic.

steps.title: Convert daily traffic to a rate
steps.html:
There are 86,400 seconds in a day.

Operation Average rate
Read 20 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231/s
Upload 1 million/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6/s

Keep these rates separate. Reads and uploads can use different resources.

Example state

Item State
Input 20 reads/user/day
Estimate ≈231 reads/s average
Decision Separate reads and writes

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. 231 reads/s on average. Flow: Users to Photo service: 20M reads/day.
diagram.caption: Divide daily requests by the number of seconds in a day.

steps.title: Allow for peak load
steps.html:
Assume peak traffic is 3× the daily average.

  • Reads: 231.5 × 3 ≈ 694/s
  • Uploads: 11.6 × 3 ≈ 35/s

Assumption. Events, regions, and retries can change the peak. Use measured traffic when available.

Example state

Item State
Input Assume 3× peak
Estimate ≈694 reads/s peak
Decision Reserve headroom

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. 694 peak reads/s. Flow: Users to Photo service: Model the 3× peak.
diagram.caption: A peak multiplier raises the capacity target above the daily average.

steps.title: Calculate ingress bandwidth
steps.html:
At 2 MB per upload:

  • Average: 11.6 uploads/s × 2 MB ≈ 23 MB/s, or 185 Mb/s.
  • 3× peak: About 69 MB/s, before protocol overhead.

Warning. Capital B means bytes. Lowercase b means bits. One byte has 8 bits.

Example state

Item State
Input 2 MB/upload
Estimate ≈23 MB/s average
Decision Size network and storage

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. 23 MB/s average ingress. Object storage (added) (in focus): Holds original images. Flow: Users to Photo service: Upload a 2 MB image. Photo service to Object storage: Store the image.
diagram.caption: Upload bytes cross the network before the service stores them.

steps.title: Calculate storage and replication
steps.html:
Each day brings 1 million uploads × 2 MB = 2 TB of logical data.

Copies Capacity for 365 days
One 730 TB
Three 2,190 TB, or 2.19 PB

This estimate excludes backups, indexes, other image sizes, and storage overhead. Count backups separately from replicas.

Example state

Item State
Input 1M uploads/day · 2 MB
Estimate 2 TB/day logical
Decision 3 copies ≈ 6 TB/day

diagram.alt: Users (context): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. Object storage (in focus): Holds original images. Replicas (added) (in focus): Additional copies. About 6 TB/day in all copies. Flow: Photo service to Object storage: Store 2 TB/day. Object storage to Replicas: Write two copies.
diagram.caption: The logical image is stored and replicated; copies increase physical capacity.

steps.title: Estimate outgoing traffic and caching
steps.html:
Clients read 20 million photos/day × 2 MB = 40 TB/day.

If caches serve 90% of the bytes, the origin serves 4 TB/day.

Note. The byte hit rate can differ from the request hit rate. A few large misses can account for most of the bytes.

Example state

Item State
Input 20M reads/day · 2 MB
Estimate 40 TB/day delivered
Decision 90% hit → 4 TB origin

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (context): Handles reads and uploads. Object storage (in focus): Holds original images. Replicas (context): Additional copies. Cache (added) (in focus): Serves repeated views. 90% byte hit rate. Flow: Users to Cache: Request a photo. Cache to Object storage: Fetch on miss. Object storage to Cache: Return original. Cache to Users: Serve the photo.
diagram.caption: The cache serves hits; misses still read from origin storage.

steps.title: Test a capacity choice
steps.html:
Assume one replica can serve 200 reads/s at the target latency.

  1. Divide peak load by capacity. 694 ÷ 200 = 3.47.
  2. Round up to 4 replicas.
  3. Use 5 replicas to keep four serving if one fails.

Check. Verify latency under concurrent load. Test uneven routing and downstream failures.

Example state

Item State
Input 694 peak reads/s
Estimate 200 reads/s per replica
Decision 5 replicas with one spare

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. Four serving + one spare. Object storage (context): Holds original images. Replicas (context): Additional copies. Cache (context): Serves repeated views. Load balancer (added) (in focus): Distributes requests. Flow: Users to Load balancer: Send peak reads. Load balancer to Photo service: Route to replicas.
diagram.caption: The load balancer distributes requests among service replicas.

steps.title: Recap: a repeatable method
steps.html:
Quantity Estimate and implication
Average reads 231/s from 20M reads/day.
Peak reads 694/s at 3×. Add headroom.
Logical storage 730 TB/year. Add copies and overhead.
Origin traffic 4 TB/day when caches serve 90% of bytes.

Write down units and assumptions before sizing. Compare the estimates with measured load.

Example state

Item State
Input Assumptions stated
Estimate 694 peak reads/s · 730 TB/year
Decision Measure and revise

diagram.alt: Users (in focus): Upload and view photos. Photo service (in focus): Handles reads and uploads. Verify peak capacity. Object storage (in focus): Holds original images. 730 TB/year logical. Replicas (in focus): Additional copies. Cache (in focus): Serves repeated views. Load balancer (in focus): Distributes requests. Flow: Users to Load balancer: Send reads. Load balancer to Photo service: Distribute requests. Photo service to Cache: Read from cache. Cache to Object storage: Fetch on miss. Object storage to Replicas: Replicate uploads.
diagram.caption: The estimates inform capacity for the service, cache, network, and storage.

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal
lessons.summary: Choose between a larger machine and more machines.

steps.title: Scale up
steps.html:
Scale up by giving one machine more resources. The report service uses all 4 vCPUs on Server A.

Give Server A 8 vCPUs. Measure the report time again.

Note. A report that uses one thread may gain little from more cores.

Example state

Item State
Server capacity More per server
Server count 1
Routing One destination

diagram.alt: Traffic (in focus): Incoming requests. Server A (in focus): First instance. 4 → 8 vCPUs. Flow: Traffic to Server A: Send all requests.
diagram.caption: Add capacity to the existing server when the workload benefits from a larger machine.

steps.title: Scale out
steps.html:
Scale out by adding machines. Run two 4-vCPU instances and split independent reports between them.

Each instance must be able to run the reports it receives.

Example state

Item State
Server capacity Capacity per server unchanged
Server count 2
Routing Split traffic

diagram.alt: Traffic (in focus): Incoming requests. Server A (in focus): First instance. Server B (added) (in focus): Second instance. Add a second instance. Flow: Traffic to Server A: Route first share. Traffic to Server B: Route second share.
diagram.caption: Both instances need to be able to process the requests sent to them.

steps.title: Choose for the bottleneck
steps.html:
Test both options at peak load. Repeat with one instance unavailable.

  • Measure CPU and memory use.
  • Check whether the database limits throughput.
  • Compare how long it takes to add capacity and recover from failure.

Example state

Item State
Server capacity Find the limit
Server count Workload dependent
Routing Check failure capacity

diagram.alt: Traffic (context): Incoming requests. Server A (in focus): First instance. Can A carry peak load alone?. Server B (in focus): Second instance. Test loss of one instance.
diagram.caption: Compare the cost and recovery impact before you choose how to scale.

lessons.title: Load Balancing
lessons.summary: Distribute requests across healthy instances.

steps.title: Find the overloaded server
steps.html:
The ticket site has two servers. All clients use Server A's address.

  • Server A: Requests arrive faster than it can finish them. A queue builds.
  • Server B: It has spare capacity. Clients send it no requests.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Server A
Policy Direct
Serving backends A

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Queue builds. Server B (context): Backend B. Spare capacity. Flow: Clients to Server A: All requests.
diagram.caption: Server B has spare capacity, but every client connects to Server A.

steps.title: Give clients one service address
steps.html:
Publish one service address. Clients send requests to the load balancer.

  1. The balancer selects a backend.
  2. It forwards the request.
  3. It relays the response.

The service address stays the same when you add or replace a backend.

Key idea. A backend pool is the group of servers to which the load balancer can send traffic.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Load balancer
Policy Pool routing
Serving backends A and B

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Load balancer (added) (in focus): Public service address. Select a healthy backend. Flow: Clients to Load balancer: Use one address. Load balancer to Server A: Forward to A. Load balancer to Server B: Forward to B.
diagram.caption: Publish the balancer address so backend addresses can change independently.

steps.title: Take turns with round robin
steps.html:
Round robin takes turns across the available servers.

Request Server
First A
Second B
Third A

The cycle repeats while both servers are available.

Key idea. This policy works best when servers have similar capacity and requests take a similar amount of work.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Load balancer
Policy Round robin
Serving backends A and B

diagram.alt: Clients (context): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Repeat A → B → A. Flow: Load balancer to Server A: First request. Load balancer to Server B: Next request.
diagram.caption: A and B take turns receiving new work when both are available.

steps.title: Compare short and long requests
steps.html:
Opening a listing is fast. Generating a report takes longer.

Each counts as one request. The report holds resources for longer, so equal request counts can leave one server busier.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Load balancer
Policy Round robin
Serving backends A and B, uneven load

diagram.alt: Clients (context): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Report holds resources longer. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Flow: Load balancer to Server A: Assign long report. Load balancer to Server B: Short listing.
diagram.caption: Equal request counts can leave one server busier when request costs differ.

steps.title: Use the number of open connections
steps.html:
Least connections sends a new connection to the server with the fewest open connections.

  • Server A: Reports still hold connections open.
  • Server B: It has fewer open connections. It receives the next one.

Key idea. Open connections approximate load. One connection can carry multiple requests, so actual server load can differ.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Load balancer
Policy Least connections
Serving backends New traffic to B

diagram.alt: Clients (context): Ticket buyers. Server A (context): Backend A. More open connections. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Fewer open connections. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Flow: Load balancer to Server B: New connection.
diagram.caption: The example favors Server B because it has fewer open connections.

steps.title: Route around an unhealthy server
steps.html:
Health checks help the balancer decide which servers can take new work.

  1. Server B fails enough checks to reach the configured threshold.
  2. The balancer stops sending it new requests.
  3. Later, successful checks can return it to the pool.

Key idea. The remaining servers need enough capacity to handle the traffic after a backend fails.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Load balancer
Policy Health checks
Serving backends A only

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Server B (context): Backend B. Failed health threshold. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Flow: Clients to Load balancer: Send new work. Load balancer to Server A: Route to healthy A. Load balancer to Server B: Health check fails.
diagram.caption: Remove Server B from rotation after it fails the health check threshold.

steps.title: Check what happens when the balancer fails
steps.html:
One load balancer sits on every request path.

Warning. If it fails, clients lose access even when both backend servers are healthy.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Unavailable
Policy No routing
Serving backends Unreachable

diagram.alt: Clients (context): Ticket buyers. Server A (context): Backend A. Backend stays healthy. Server B (context): Backend B. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Public route unavailable.
diagram.caption: Both backends can still be healthy while the public entry point is down.

steps.title: Prepare a standby load balancer
steps.html:
Restore the primary balancer. Give a standby the same routing rules and backend pool.

  • Primary: Serves the public address.
  • Standby: Checks the primary. It waits until needed.

Put the standby in a separate failure domain so a single host or network failure is less likely to stop both.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Primary + standby
Policy Primary serves
Serving backends A and B

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Load balancer (in focus): Public service address. Primary restored. Standby balancer (added) (in focus): Separate failure zone. Ready in a separate zone. Flow: Clients to Load balancer: Public address. Load balancer to Server A: Forward new work. Load balancer to Server B: Forward new work. Standby balancer to Load balancer: Probe primary.
diagram.caption: The primary serves the public address. The new standby waits in a separate failure zone.

steps.title: Test the switch to standby
steps.html:
The primary fails again. The standby takes over the service address, or a routing service directs traffic to it.

New requests can reach the same backends. Measure how long the switch takes and check whether existing connections survive.

Key idea. Measure the switch time and the effect on open connections. Some clients may need to reconnect.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Standby serves
Policy Routing restored
Serving backends A and B

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Load balancer (context): Public service address. Primary unavailable. Standby balancer (in focus): Separate failure zone. Now serving new connections. Flow: Clients to Standby balancer: Fail over. Standby balancer to Server A: Forward to A. Standby balancer to Server B: Forward to B.
diagram.caption: Measure how long the public address takes to work again after failover.

steps.title: Route by HTTP path
steps.html:
An HTTP load balancer can choose a backend pool by request path.

Path Backend pool
/listings Listing pool, starting with Server A
/reports Report pool, starting with Server B

Size each pool for its own workload.

Example state

Item State
Entry point Standby serves
Policy HTTP path
Serving backends Listing and report pools

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Ticket buyers. Server A (in focus): Backend A. Listing pool. Server B (in focus): Backend B. Report pool. Load balancer (context): Public service address. Standby balancer (in focus): Separate failure zone. Flow: Clients to Standby balancer: Request ticket data. Standby balancer to Server A: Route /listings. lessons.title: Stateless Services
lessons.summary: Make requests portable across service instances.

steps.html:
Send a session ID or a signed token with every request.

A healthy replica can handle the request without relying on an earlier request to the same process.

Some sessions need shared data that can change. Store it outside the service replicas.

  • Set an expiry for session records.
  • Give access only to the services that need it.

Restart one replica during a series of requests. Send the next request to another healthy replica.

lessons.summary: Serve repeated reads faster while managing stale data.

  • Miss: Read the database. Save a copy with an expiry.

steps.html:

  • Check what other readers or writers can see while that transaction runs.

lessons.summary: Trade write cost and storage for faster lookups.

The query filters on customer_id = 42. An index on customer_id lets the database find matching entries.

You need recent orders for one customer. Try an index on (customer_id, created_at).

An insert or update must maintain the affected indexes.

lessons.title: Storage Engines
lessons.summary: Compare common read and write paths.

steps.title: B-tree storage
steps.html:
A B-tree keeps keys in sorted pages.

  • For one key, follow the tree to the matching page.
  • For a range, scan nearby entries in order.
  • A write can change one or more pages.

steps.title: Log-structured storage
steps.html:
A log-structured merge tree (LSM tree) buffers writes in memory. It later writes them to sorted files.

  • Compaction merges files and removes obsolete values.

Item State
Bytes path Validation and worker
Metadata Track processing state
Access state Ready after checks

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): Uploads and downloads. Object storage (in focus): File bytes. Metadata DB (in focus): Ownership and object key. Pending → ready after checks. File API (in focus): Authorizes file access. Flow: Client to Object storage: Upload file. File API to Metadata DB: Mark file ready.
diagram.caption: The metadata record becomes ready only after validation completes.

lessons.title: REST, RPC & GraphQL
lessons.summary: Compare ways services expose operations and data.

steps.title: Choose a contract
steps.html:
Compare three ways to return the same order:

Interface Example
Resource-oriented HTTP Read /orders/42.
RPC Call GetOrder.
GraphQL Request the fields needed for order 42.

Choose the contract that fits the clients.

Example state

Item State
Contract REST, RPC, or GraphQL
Design focus Resources, operations, fields
Check Match client needs

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): API consumer. API (in focus): Public contract. Choose request and response. Service (in focus): Implements the operation. Flow: Client to API: GET /orders/42. API to Service: Load order 42.
diagram.caption: Compare how a client would make the same request with each interface.

steps.title: Plan evolution
steps.html:
Define the schema, error responses, and pagination.

Add a new field as optional first. Test the old client against the new API.

Example state

Item State
Contract Versioned contract
Design focus Compatible changes
Check Test older clients

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): API consumer. API (in focus): Public contract. Keep old clients compatible. Service (context): Implements the operation. Flow: Client to API: List with cursor.
diagram.caption: Add a new field before you remove one that deployed clients still use.

steps.title: Operate the API
steps.html:
For each request:

  1. Authenticate the caller.
  2. Check access to the order.
  3. Apply a deadline.
  4. Record latency and outcome.

Example state

Item State
Contract Running API
Design focus Deadlines and limits
Check Observe failures

diagram.alt: Client (context): API consumer. API (in focus): Public contract. Check caller and deadline. Service (in focus): Implements the operation. Flow: API to Service: Send with deadline.
diagram.caption: Apply authentication and rate limits at the entry point and authorization where the action is enforced.

lessons.title: Message Queues
lessons.summary: Decouple work from the request path.

steps.title: Enqueue work
steps.html:
The order API places a confirmation email job on a queue. It can respond before a worker sends the email.

Measure how long jobs wait during a burst.

Example state

Item State
Work state Queued
Worker action Claim available jobs
Failure path Delay during a burst

diagram.alt: Producer (in focus): Submits jobs. Queue (in focus): Buffers work. Absorb a burst. Worker (in focus): Processes jobs. Flow: Producer to Queue: Enqueue email job. Queue to Worker: Deliver when ready.
diagram.caption: Track the oldest queued job to see when workers fall behind.

steps.title: Process reliably
steps.html:
Acknowledge a job after you record success.

Warning. A lost acknowledgment can cause redelivery. Use a stable job ID and make the email operation safe to retry.

Example state

Item State
Work state In progress
Worker action Acknowledge after success
Failure path Possible redelivery

diagram.alt: Producer (context): Submits jobs. Queue (in focus): Buffers work. Worker (in focus): Processes jobs. Deduplicate by job ID. Flow: Queue to Worker: Deliver or retry. Worker to Queue: Acknowledge job.
diagram.caption: Make the job safe to run again if the worker finishes but loses its acknowledgment.

steps.title: Handle failures
steps.html:
• Retry temporary failures with a limit.
  • Move jobs that exceed the limit to a dead-letter queue.
  • Inspect or replay these jobs with safeguards against duplicate effects.

Example state

Item State
Work state Retried
Worker action Back off
Failure path Dead-letter after limit

diagram.alt: Producer (context): Submits jobs. Queue (in focus): Buffers work. Worker (in focus): Processes jobs. Dead-letter queue (added) (in focus): Holds failed jobs. Keep error details. Flow: Queue to Worker: Retry the job. Worker to Queue: Report failure. Queue to Dead-letter queue: Move after retries.
diagram.caption: Keep enough context to investigate a failed job before you replay it.

lessons.title: Pub/Sub & Events
lessons.summary: Send events to multiple independent consumers.

steps.title: Publish an event
steps.html:
The order service publishes one OrderPlaced event.

The email and analytics subscriptions each receive a copy. Each processes it at its own pace.

Example state

Item State
Event path Broker fans out
Consumers Independent subscribers
Design check Producer can continue

diagram.alt: Publisher (in focus): Emits business events. Event broker (in focus): Routes and retains events. Consumers (in focus): Independent subscriptions. Email and analytics. Flow: Publisher to Event broker: Publish OrderPlaced. Event broker to Consumers: Deliver event.
diagram.caption: Each subscriber can handle a different task triggered by the same event.

steps.title: Design the event
steps.html:
Include the event ID, schema version, and fields consumers need.

Warning. Leave unnecessary personal data out of the event.

Example state

Item State
Event path Versioned event
Consumers Read supported fields
Design check Stable event ID

diagram.alt: Publisher (in focus): Emits business events. Include event version. Event broker (in focus): Routes and retains events. Consumers (context): Independent subscriptions. Flow: Publisher to Event broker: Event ID + version.
diagram.caption: Avoid requiring every subscriber to upgrade when a publisher adds a field.

steps.title: Expect duplicates
steps.html:
Test redelivery to both subscriptions. Use the event ID to avoid repeating side effects.

Define ordering, replay behavior, and retention for each subscription.

Example state

Item State
Event path Redelivery possible
Consumers Deduplicate or replay
Design check Check ordering scope

diagram.alt: Publisher (context): Emits business events. Event broker (in focus): Routes and retains events. Consumers (in focus): Independent subscriptions. Apply the event ID once. Flow: Event broker to Consumers: Repeat OrderPlaced.
diagram.caption: Use event IDs and the broker’s ordering guarantees to handle repeated delivery.

lessons.title: Real-time Updates
lessons.summary: Deliver changes to clients with an appropriate connection model.

steps.title: Poll for changes
steps.html:
A dashboard can poll every 5 seconds.

  • Short intervals reduce the wait for updates.
  • Short intervals also create more requests when there is no change.

Example state

Item State
Connection Periodic requests
Update delivery At next poll
Recovery Poll again

diagram.alt: Server (in focus): Source of updates. Client (in focus): Displays updates. One poll per interval. Flow: Client to Server: Poll for changes. Server to Client: Return latest state.
diagram.caption: A shorter interval reduces wait time and increases request volume.

steps.title: Keep a connection
steps.html:
Choose When
Server-sent events The server pushes one-way updates over HTTP.
WebSocket The client and the server both send messages.

Example state

Item State
Connection Long-lived
Update delivery Push or duplex
Recovery Detect disconnect

diagram.alt: Server (in focus): Source of updates. Connection (added) (in focus): Persistent update stream. SSE or WebSocket. Client (in focus): Displays updates. Flow: Client to Connection: Open stream. Server to Connection: Publish update. Connection to Client: Push update.
diagram.caption: Use a bidirectional connection when the client and server both need to send updates independently.

steps.title: Recover after disconnect
steps.html:
After a disconnect, send the last processed sequence. Ask the server for later updates.

Fetch a new snapshot if the server no longer keeps the required updates.

Example state

Item State
Connection Reconnecting
Update delivery Resume or resync
Recovery Sequence or snapshot

diagram.alt: Server (in focus): Source of updates. Connection (in focus): Persistent update stream. Client (in focus): Displays updates. Resume from the last ID. Flow: Client to Connection: Reconnect with ID. Server to Connection: Replay or snapshot. Connection to Client: Catch the client up.
diagram.caption: If missed updates are no longer available, fetch a fresh snapshot.

lessons.title: Redundancy & Failover
lessons.summary: Reduce the effect of component failures.

steps.title: Remove single points
steps.html:
Put the standby in a separate zone. Replicate the state it needs.

Warning. Shared dependencies can still stop both copies. Check shared networks, services, and control systems.

Example state

Item State
Serving path Primary
Standby state Ready in another zone
Recovery check Independent failures

diagram.alt: Traffic (in focus): Incoming requests. Active (in focus): Serving in zone A. Standby (in focus): Ready in zone B. Separate failure domain. Flow: Traffic to Active: Serve requests. Active to Standby: Replicate state.
diagram.caption: Place the standby where a failure of the primary is less likely to affect it.

steps.title: Detect and fail over
steps.html:
1. Detect the failure with health checks.
  2. Stop the old active instance from taking work.
  3. Send requests to the standby.

Measure how long the change takes.

Example state

Item State
Serving path Standby after switch
Standby state Takes over
Recovery check Detect and reroute

diagram.alt: Traffic (in focus): Incoming requests. Active (in focus): Serving in zone A. Stop routing to zone A. Standby (in focus): Ready in zone B. Promote in zone B. Flow: Traffic to Standby: Route to standby.
diagram.caption: Separate failure detection time from the time it takes to route requests again.

steps.title: Test recovery
steps.html:
During a failover drill, measure:

  • Recovery time: How long before requests work again?
  • Data loss: Which writes survived?

Compare both results with the recovery objectives.

Example state

Item State
Serving path Test traffic
Standby state Exercise the switch
Recovery check Measure recovery time

diagram.alt: Traffic (in focus): Incoming requests. Active (context): Serving in zone A. Standby (in focus): Ready in zone B. Measure time and data loss. Flow: Traffic to Standby: Check recovery.
diagram.caption: Run a failover exercise with a workload that resembles normal traffic.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting
lessons.summary: Protect finite capacity by controlling request rates.

steps.title: Set a limit
steps.html:
Choose how many reports each user can request. Use an authenticated user ID when available.

Set the rate to a level the service can handle.

Example state

Item State
Scope Per caller
Decision Check allowance
Client signal Permit within limit

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Requests by identity. Limiter (in focus): Budget decision. Key the limit by user. Service (in focus): Protected endpoint. Flow: Clients to Limiter: Check user budget. Limiter to Service: Forward request.
diagram.caption: Set the scope based on the resource to protect. A per-user limit and a service-wide limit protect different resources.

steps.title: Choose an algorithm
steps.html:
A bucket holds 10 tokens and adds 2 tokens per second. Each accepted request uses one token.

An idle user with a full bucket can send 10 requests at once.

Example state

Item State
Scope Bucket or window
Decision Allow or reject
Client signal Bursts depend on policy

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Requests by identity. Limiter (in focus): Budget decision. Refill at 2 tokens per second. Service (context): Protected endpoint. Flow: Clients to Limiter: Burst requests.
diagram.caption: A token bucket can allow a short burst when tokens have accumulated.

steps.title: Return useful feedback
steps.html:
Return HTTP 429 when the budget runs out. Include retry guidance when you can calculate it.

Decision. If several limiters share a budget, decide how they behave when the budget store is unavailable.

Example state

Item State
Scope Caller over limit
Decision Reject
Client signal HTTP 429

diagram.alt: Clients (in focus): Requests by identity. Limiter (in focus): Budget decision. Service receives no request. Service (context): Protected endpoint. Flow: Clients to Limiter: Send over limit. Limiter to Clients: 429 + Retry-After.
diagram.caption: Return retry guidance when the service knows when the caller can try again.

lessons.title: Timeouts & Retries
lessons.summary: Bound waiting and avoid amplifying failures.

steps.title: Set a deadline
steps.html:
Give the full request a deadline of 800 ms.

Allow up to 500 ms for the downstream call. Keep 300 ms for other work and the response.

Example state

Item State
Request budget Overall deadline
Attempt First attempt
Safety check Bound the wait

diagram.alt: Caller (in focus): Client or upstream service. Service (in focus): Handles requests. Reserve time for the response. Dependency (in focus): Downstream operation. Flow: Caller to Service: 800 ms deadline. Service to Dependency: 500 ms budget.
diagram.caption: Give downstream calls enough time to finish within the caller’s remaining deadline.

steps.title: Retry carefully
steps.html:
Retry only a suitable failure and only while time remains. Use backoff and jitter to spread retries over time.

Warning. A timeout can occur after the server has completed the write.

Example state

Item State
Request budget Remaining time
Attempt Backoff with jitter
Safety check Bounded retries

diagram.alt: Caller (in focus): Client or upstream service. Back off with jitter. Service (in focus): Handles requests. Dependency (context): Downstream operation. Flow: Caller to Service: Retry if time left.
diagram.caption: Retry short-lived failures only while enough time remains for another attempt.

steps.title: Prevent duplicate effects
steps.html:
Reuse the same idempotency key for retries of a write.

  • Store the result with the effect when possible.
  • Reject the same key if the new payload differs.

Example state

Item State
Request budget Shared deadline
Attempt Possible duplicate
Safety check Check idempotency key

diagram.alt: Caller (in focus): Client or upstream service. Service (in focus): Handles requests. Keep the prior result. Dependency (in focus): Downstream operation. Flow: Caller to Service: Reuse write key. Service to Dependency: Apply once.
diagram.caption: A timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. A stable key can let the server recognize another attempt at the same operation.

lessons.title: Observability
lessons.summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand system behavior.

steps.title: Measure symptoms
steps.html:
Measure what the shopper sees:

  • Success rate: The share of valid checkout requests that succeed.
  • Latency: How long the shopper waits.

Use traffic and resource saturation to diagnose problems.

Example state

Item State
Signal Metrics
Scope Service health
Operator action Check errors and latency

diagram.alt: Services (in focus): User request paths. Telemetry (in focus): Metrics, traces, logs. Measure user-visible success. Flow: Services to Telemetry: Latency and errors.
diagram.caption: Measure the rate of failed and slow requests from the caller’s point of view.

steps.title: Follow a request
steps.html:
Send a trace ID between services. Use it to match spans and logs for a slow checkout.

Warning. Keep secrets out of telemetry.

Example state

Item State
Signal Trace
Scope One request
Operator action Find the slow span

diagram.alt: Services (in focus): User request paths. Telemetry (in focus): Metrics, traces, logs. Carry a trace ID. Operators (added) (in focus): Investigate and respond. Flow: Services to Telemetry: Emit trace spans. Telemetry to Operators: Inspect trace.
diagram.caption: Follow the same request across components to see where it waited.

steps.title: Act on signals
steps.html:
Alert when checkout failures spend the error budget too fast.

Use traces and logs to find the affected dependency. Test that telemetry still works during outages.

Example state

Item State
Signal Alert and dashboard
Scope User impact
Operator action Confirm the cause

diagram.alt: Services (context): User request paths. Telemetry (in focus): Metrics, traces, logs. Operators (in focus): Investigate and respond. Trace user impact. Flow: Telemetry to Operators: Alert on errors.
diagram.caption: Alert on a symptom that needs a response. Use traces and logs to investigate it.

lessons.title: Monolith vs Microservices
lessons.summary: Choose service boundaries based on real needs.

steps.title: Start with boundaries
steps.html:
Start with order and invoice modules in one deployment.

Give each module a clear interface. This limits the effect of changes on the other module.

Example state

Item State
Deployment One application
Call path In-process modules
Design check Keep clear interfaces

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): Uses the public API. Application (in focus): Initial modular deployment. Use a module interface. Data (in focus): Application-owned records. Flow: Client to Application: Request an invoice. Application to Data: Read invoices.
diagram.caption: Module boundaries make it possible to understand the responsibilities inside a single deployment.

steps.title: Compare costs
steps.html:
Extract the invoice module if it needs independent releases or scaling.

  • Assign data ownership.
  • Define how to handle timeouts and failures between services.
  • Add monitoring for the new request path.

Example state

Item State
Deployment Separate services
Call path Network calls
Design check Handle partial failure

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): Uses the public API. Application (in focus): Initial modular deployment. Data (in focus): Application-owned records. Invoice service (added) (in focus): Extracted deployment. Own invoice behavior and data. Flow: Client to Application: Request an invoice. Application to Invoice service: Request invoice. Invoice service to Data: Read owned data.
diagram.caption: The invoice service is a separate deployment with ownership of invoice data.

steps.title: Evolve deliberately
steps.html:
Compare release lead time and failure rates before and after extraction.

Keep the modules together if the new deployment boundary adds more work than it saves.

Example state

Item State
Deployment Split if justified
Call path Selected boundary
Design check Measure the benefit

diagram.alt: Client (context): Uses the public API. Application (in focus): Initial modular deployment. Compare release and runtime costs. Data (context): Application-owned records. Invoice service (in focus): Extracted deployment. Flow: Application to Invoice service: Measure call cost.
diagram.caption: A team can extract a part that needs its own release cycle or scaling policy.

lessons.title: Service Discovery
lessons.summary: Find healthy service instances as they change.

steps.title: Register instances
steps.html:
An instance registers its address when it starts.

The registry removes the entry when the instance stops or fails health checks.

Example state

Item State
Registry Instances register
Caller view Addresses become known
Risk Stale entries

diagram.alt: Registry (in focus): Current endpoint list. Expire stale entries. Instances (in focus): Available service endpoints. Flow: Instances to Registry: Register endpoint.
diagram.caption: Remove instances that can no longer serve traffic.

steps.title: Resolve a destination
steps.html:
1. Look up the service name.
  2. Select one listed endpoint.
  3. Send the request.

Example state

Item State
Registry Lookup
Caller view Select a listed address
Risk Endpoint can change

diagram.alt: Caller (added) (in focus): Service or proxy. Pick an available endpoint. Registry (in focus): Current endpoint list. Instances (in focus): Available service endpoints. Flow: Caller to Registry: Find payment API. Registry to Caller: Healthy endpoints. Caller to Instances: Call instance.
diagram.caption: The caller or proxy selects a healthy endpoint from the available addresses.

steps.title: Handle stale results
steps.html:
A cached address can point to an instance that is gone. Refresh the list when the entry is stale.

Retry only when the operation is safe to repeat and the deadline leaves enough time.

Example state

Item State
Registry Cached lookup
Caller view Entry may be stale
Risk Retry with fresh data

diagram.alt: Caller (in focus): Service or proxy. Retry within the deadline. Registry (in focus): Current endpoint list. Instances (context): Available service endpoints. Flow: Caller to Registry: Refresh on failure. Registry to Caller: Return endpoints.
diagram.caption: Refresh the list when a selected endpoint no longer accepts connections.

lessons.title: Sagas & Distributed Tx
lessons.summary: Use a saga to coordinate a distributed transaction across services.

steps.title: Break work into steps
steps.html:
The order workflow charges the payment, then reserves stock. Each service commits its own change locally.

Record each result before you continue.

Example state

Item State
Workflow Order started
Local effect Payment and inventory steps
Recovery Record progress

diagram.alt: Order workflow (in focus): Tracks local steps. Record each step result. Payment (in focus): Authorizes or refunds. Inventory (in focus): Reserves stock. Flow: Order workflow to Payment: Charge the payment. Order workflow to Inventory: Reserve stock.
diagram.caption: Each service commits its own change. Keep the outcome of each step so a retry can continue safely.

steps.title: Compensate failures
steps.html:
If the payment succeeds and the stock reservation fails, request a refund. This is a compensating action.

Warning. The refund can also fail. Record its outcome for retry or manual follow-up.

Example state

Item State
Workflow Reservation failed
Local effect Payment already applied
Recovery Refund when possible

diagram.alt: Order workflow (in focus): Tracks local steps. Payment (in focus): Authorizes or refunds. Refund is a separate action. Inventory (in focus): Reserves stock. Flow: Inventory to Order workflow: Reservation failed. Order workflow to Payment: Request refund.
diagram.caption: A refund is a new action with its own result. Record its success or failure.

steps.title: Make progress visible
steps.html:
Give each step a stable ID. Make each effect safe to repeat.

Store workflow state so a recovered worker can continue. Operators can use the same state to inspect a stuck order.

Example state

Item State
Workflow Workflow tracked
Local effect Duplicate events possible
Recovery Resume or inspect

diagram.alt: Order workflow (in focus): Tracks local steps. Persist saga progress. Payment (in focus): Authorizes or refunds. Inventory (in focus): Reserves stock. Flow: Order workflow to Payment: Resume payment. Order workflow to Inventory: Resume reservation.
diagram.caption: Store the current step so an operator can tell which actions still need attention.

lessons.title: Batch & Stream Processing
lessons.summary: Choose how and when to process incoming data.

steps.title: Process in batches
steps.html:
A batch job runs on a schedule. It reads yesterday's completed order files and publishes the daily sales total.

Example state

Item State
Processing Batch
Input boundary Bounded input
Result Scheduled output

diagram.alt: Events (in focus): Input records. Processor (in focus): Aggregates results. Bounded input by day. Output (in focus): Published totals. Flow: Events to Processor: Read daily files. Processor to Output: Publish daily total.
diagram.caption: Choose a batch when the result can wait until the next scheduled run.

steps.title: Process a stream
steps.html:
A stream updates sales totals as orders arrive.

Use the event time. Decide whether late orders can change totals that you have already published.

Example state

Item State
Processing Stream
Input boundary Arriving events
Result Incremental updates

diagram.alt: Events (in focus): Input records. Processor (in focus): Aggregates results. Define allowed lateness. Output (in focus): Published totals. Flow: Events to Processor: Stream orders. Processor to Output: Update window total.
diagram.caption: Define how late events affect results that may already have been published.

steps.title: Define correctness
steps.html:
Recover from a checkpoint and replay the same events.

Use event IDs or a stable output key to prevent a restart from counting an order twice.

Example state

Item State
Processing Starts again after failure
Input boundary Checkpoint or replay
Result Verify duplicate handling

diagram.alt: Events (in focus): Input records. Processor (in focus): Aggregates results. Output (in focus): Published totals. Upsert by window ID. Flow: Events to Processor: Replay checkpoint. Processor to Output: Idempotent write.
diagram.caption: Test recovery with the same inputs to check whether it changes the result.

lessons.title: Authentication
lessons.summary: Verify who is making a request.

steps.title: Verify identity
steps.html:
Use a standard protocol such as OpenID Connect and a maintained client library.

The identity provider verifies the user's sign-in.

Example state

Item State
Identity check Credentials or provider
Request state Unverified to verified
Defense Validate proof

diagram.alt: User (in focus): Person with a browser. Identity provider (in focus): Verifies identity. Verify credentials or passkey. Flow: User to Identity provider: Authenticate.
diagram.caption: An application can delegate login to an identity provider and verify its response.

steps.title: Maintain a session
steps.html:
Validate the identity result before you create a session. Use a secure session cookie when appropriate.

Define expiry, revocation, and what happens when the user signs out.

Example state

Item State
Identity check Session or token
Request state Authenticated
Defense Expire or revoke

diagram.alt: User (in focus): Person with a browser. Identity provider (in focus): Verifies identity. Application (added) (in focus): Creates its own session. Validate proof and expiry. Flow: Identity provider to Application: Identity result. Application to User: Set session cookie.
diagram.caption: Set a lifetime that matches the amount of time a session remains useful.

steps.title: Defend the entry point
steps.html:
Use rate limits and strong authentication where the risk calls for them.

Test both paths. Account recovery must protect the account as carefully as sign-in.

Example state

Item State
Identity check Login entry point
Request state May reject attempts
Defense MFA and rate limits

diagram.alt: User (in focus): Person with a browser. Identity provider (in focus): Verifies identity. Limit repeated attempts. Application (context): Creates its own session. Flow: User to Identity provider: Use passkey.
diagram.caption: Use multiple factors where appropriate to limit the impact of a stolen password.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.summary: Decide which actions an identity may perform.

steps.title: Check the action
steps.html:
Before updating an order, check:

  • Who is making the request?
  • Which action are they asking to perform?
  • Who owns the order?

Example state

Item State
Identity Known caller
Policy scope Action and resource
Outcome Allow or deny

diagram.alt: Identity (in focus): Known caller and action. Policy (in focus): Server-side decision. Check action and owner. Resource (in focus): Protected order. Flow: Identity to Policy: Can edit order 42?. Policy to Resource: Apply if allowed.
diagram.caption: A user who can update their own record may need separate permission to update someone else’s.

steps.title: Apply least privilege
steps.html:
Give support staff only the permissions they need.

A role can permit an action. The API still needs to check the tenant or owner for the specific order.

Example state

Item State
Identity Role or attribute
Policy scope Required permissions
Outcome Least privilege

diagram.alt: Identity (in focus): Known caller and action. Policy (in focus): Server-side decision. Allow read, deny edits. Resource (context): Protected order. Flow: Identity to Policy: Check support role.
diagram.caption: Keep permissions limited to the actions a role needs.

steps.title: Enforce on the server
steps.html:
Enforce authorization on the server for each protected request.

Test. Change the order ID. The caller must be unable to read or change another tenant's order.

Example state

Item State
Identity Server check
Policy scope Every protected action
Outcome Reject if denied

diagram.alt: Identity (in focus): Known caller and action. Policy (in focus): Server-side decision. Deny before touching order. Resource (context): Protected order. Flow: Identity to Policy: Request update.
diagram.caption: Apply the policy at the trusted service before it reads or changes the resource.

lessons.title: Encryption & Secrets
lessons.summary: Protect data and manage keys separately from code.

steps.title: Protect data in transit
steps.html:
Use TLS when a connection carries sensitive data. Verify the certificate and the endpoint identity.

Choose encryption at rest based on who can access the stored data and how sensitive it is.

Example state

Item State
Protection In transit
Material Certificates and keys
Check Verify peer

diagram.alt: Client (in focus): Caller verifies the peer. Verify server identity. Service (in focus): Processes protected data. Flow: Client to Service: Verified TLS.
diagram.caption: Use TLS on connections that carry sensitive data and verify the endpoint identity.

steps.title: Manage secrets
steps.html:
The service retrieves secrets with a scoped identity. Grant access only to the secrets that service needs.

Warning. Keep credentials out of code and logs.

Example state

Item State
Protection Stored credentials
Material Managed secret
Check Restrict retrieval

diagram.alt: Client (context): Caller verifies the peer. Service (in focus): Processes protected data. Secret store (added) (in focus): Controls credentials and keys. Grant access to service identity. Flow: Service to Secret store: Get scoped secret. Secret store to Service: Return credential.
diagram.caption: The service can retrieve its credential at runtime. Keep credential values out of logs and code.

steps.title: Rotate and audit
steps.html:
1. Create the replacement credential.
  2. Verify that the service can use it.
  3. Revoke the old credential.

Record retrievals so you can investigate unexpected access.

Example state

Item State
Protection Key lifecycle
Material Rotate and revoke
Check Audit access

diagram.alt: Client (context): Caller verifies the peer. Service (in focus): Processes protected data. Switch before retiring old key. Secret store (in focus): Controls credentials and keys. Flow: Service to Secret store: Get new key.
diagram.caption: Verify that services can switch to a new key before you retire the old one.

lessons.title: Testing
lessons.summary: Verify behavior at the right levels.

steps.title: Test behavior
steps.html:
Test Example
Unit Check checkout price rules.
Integration Verify the database constraint that prevents duplicate orders.

Example state

Item State
Scope Unit and integration
Example check Logic and boundaries
Feedback Fast checks first

diagram.alt: Unit (in focus): Checks focused logic. Cover discount rules. Integration (in focus): Checks real boundaries. Flow: Unit to Integration: Check constraints.
diagram.caption: Verify behavior at the layer where a failure is easiest to reproduce.

steps.title: Test the system
steps.html:
Run a full purchase from the browser through storage.

Add a load test if peak traffic is a risk. Add a failure test if a dependency outage can change the outcome.

Example state

Item State
Scope End to end

steps.title: Define the brief
steps.html:
Users need to:

  • Submit a long URL and receive a short link.
  • Open the short link and reach its destination.
  • Set expiry and see click counts.

Priority: Keep redirects fast and available. Click counts can arrive later.

steps.html:

steps.html:
1. Reserve ID blocks in a durable allocator. Each server gets a distinct block.
  2. Encode an ID in base 62.
  3. Write the code and destination to the store.

For example, 125 = 2 × 62 + 1, which encodes as 21 with digits first. Seven characters give 3.52 trillion values for the assumed 6 billion links.

Warning. Reserve blocks atomically. Never reuse a reserved block after a crash. Enforce uniqueness in the store, including for custom aliases.

steps.html:
Build a chronological feed of posts from followed accounts.

  • People can publish, read, and page through posts.
  • A post can become private or be deleted.
  • New posts should appear within seconds. A short delay is acceptable.

Ranking, ads, and media storage are out of scope. Keep the read path available. Show only posts whose access you can verify.

steps.title: Handle popular authors
steps.html:
One post from an account with 10 million followers needs 10 million insertions if you push it to every feed.

At 20,000 insertions/s, that takes 500 seconds before retries or contention. The goal is seconds.

  • Ordinary authors: Push references into follower feeds.
  • Popular authors: Pull recent posts at read time.

Set the threshold from measured cost and latency. Test strategy changes for missing or duplicate posts.

steps.title: Page without losing position
steps.html:
Use a stable cursor, such as (created_at, post_id).

  1. Fetch candidates from prepared feeds and popular timelines.
  2. Merge the results and remove duplicates.
  3. Return the next 20 permitted posts.

Define a snapshot boundary for new posts. Store enough merge state in the cursor to resume across sources.

steps.title: Enforce access and deletion
steps.html:
A feed reference can outlive an unfollow, deletion, or privacy change. Treat it as a candidate. Check current visibility before returning the post.

Warning. If the policy service is unavailable, withhold posts you cannot verify. Fetch more candidates only up to a defined limit.

Remove old entries in the background to reduce wasted work.

steps.html:

Pull popular posts Avoid millions of inserts for one post. Do more at read time.
Use stable cursors Resume across pages. Define snapshot and duplicate rules.
Check current access Protect private content. Adds a read-path dependency.
Make fan-out safe to retry Recover from worker failure. Track lag and repeats.

lessons.title: Design a Chat System
lessons.summary: Design messaging from the delivery contract through persistence, reconnects, and scale.

steps.title: Define the contract
steps.html:
Support one-to-one text messages, online delivery, and catch-up after reconnect.

  • Keep messages for one year.
  • Define an order within each conversation.
  • Acknowledge acceptance only after the server saves the message.

Use authorization and transport encryption. End-to-end encryption and exactly-once delivery are outside this example.

Item State
Traffic Estimate next
Delivery Persist then deliver

steps.title: Estimate load and storage
steps.html:
Assume 10 million daily active users. Each sends 100 messages/day.

Quantity Estimate

3× peak About 34,722/s
Logical storage 1 billion/day × 365 × 1 KB = 365 TB
Three copies About 1.1 PB

Assumption. Each stored message uses 1 KB. Add indexes, backups, and storage overhead. Attachments are out of scope.

steps.title: Keep an online connection
steps.html:
Use a persistent connection such as WebSocket. The gateway authenticates clients and holds sender and recipient connections. Revalidate sessions when required. The chat service can scale separately.

2 million connections ÷ 50,000 per gateway = 40 gateways before headroom.

Allow for failures and uneven load. Test memory, file descriptors, network use, and heartbeat costs.

steps.title: Persist before acknowledging
steps.html:
The client sends a message ID, conversation ID, and body.

  1. Check conversation membership.
  2. Assign a sequence and persist the message.
  3. Acknowledge acceptance after the durable write.

Use a unique key for the sender and client message ID. A retry with the same payload returns the prior result and sequence. Define how long to keep the key.

Note. Acceptance means the server saved the message. The recipient may still be offline.

steps.title: Route to online recipients
steps.html:
1. Save the message and its outbox record in one transaction.
  2. A relay publishes an event to the delivery queue.
  3. A worker looks up the recipient's current gateway.
  4. The gateway pushes the message.

Warning. A connection can disappear between lookup and send. Retry when useful. Clients can recover from durable history. Consumers must handle repeated events after a relay failure.

steps.title: Recover after reconnect
steps.html:
On reconnect, the client sends the last contiguous sequence it saved. The service returns later messages in pages.

  • Deduplicate by message ID.
  • Advance the cursor only after saving a contiguous range.
  • Report a gap if retention removed messages in that range.

A lost acknowledgment can cause delivery of the same message again.

steps.title: Preserve conversation order
steps.html:
Two users can send at the same time. Assign increasing sequences per conversation. Use one owner or an atomic storage operation.

Order messages by that sequence. Coordinate sequence assignment with the write so failures leave a clear result.

Note. A busy group can overload its own partition. Measure that load before changing how the system assigns ownership.

steps.title: Secure and operate the service
steps.html:
• Encrypt traffic in transit and protect stored data.
  • Authorize every send and history request.
  • Limit abusive traffic and expire messages on schedule.

Warning. A removed member must stop receiving new messages, even on an existing connection.

Monitor write latency, queue age, delivery lag, connection churn, and reconnect errors. Test both gateway and store outages.

Persistent gateway connections Deliver quickly to online users. Manage open connections.
Save before accepting Recover messages after failure. Adds write latency.
Make retries safe Handle lost acknowledgments. Keep duplicate-check state.
Sequence per conversation Give clients a stable order. Watch for busy partitions.
Resume with a cursor Recover missed messages. Handle retention gaps.
Check membership Protect sends and reads. Adds a policy check.

Measure message size, concurrency, retention, and recovery behavior before sizing the service.
